title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 109: The Saffron Crocus: The Golden Spice
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 109 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

The Saffron Crocus: The Golden Spice

Paragraph 1. Harvested from the crimson stigmas of Crocus sativus, saffron has long been prized as the world's costliest agricultural product by weight. Known historically as 'vegetable gold', this spice has influenced cooking, medicine, and royal rituals across three continents for over three thousand years. Unlike its wild relatives, the cultivated saffron crocus is a sterile plant incapable of producing seeds or spreading naturally in open fields. Instead, its survival depends entirely on human growers, who propagate the crop through the manual division and replanting of underground corms—the compact bulb-like organs that rest dormant between growing seasons.

Paragraph 2. Saffron's extraordinary price stems directly from its severe harvesting constraints. Each purple flower produces only three thin stigmas, which must be removed carefully from the open centre. The entire harvest is squeezed into an intense two-to-three-week window in late autumn. Crucially, the flowers open at dawn and begin wilting rapidly as daytime temperatures climb; field workers must gather every flower by hand before sunrise, because direct midday sunlight breaks down volatile chemical compounds and degrades essential oils. Producing a single kilogram of dried saffron requires harvesting 150,000 to 200,000 blossoms during roughly forty hours of exhausting manual work.

Paragraph 3. Archaeological discoveries confirm that saffron farming began during the Aegean Bronze Age. Brightly painted frescoes uncovered at the prehistoric site of Akrotiri, on the volcanic island of Santorini, show young women gathering crocus flowers into woven reed baskets for seasonal ceremonies. In classical Rome, saffron essence scented public bathhouses and was scattered across stone arenas to disguise the smell of gladiatorial contests, while wealthy brides wore radiant saffron-yellow wedding veils.

Paragraph 4. Throughout the medieval period, saffron regularly exceeded pure gold in value, turning European markets into battlegrounds against fraud. Because shredded stigmas were easy to imitate, dishonest merchants frequently soaked batches in honey or oil to artificially boost shipment weight, or diluted supplies with shredded marigold petals and dyed silk. In response, European city-states enacted severe laws. In Nuremberg, Germany, municipal authorities created the Safranschau—a specialised tribunal empowered to seize and chemically test every batch entering city gates, condemning convicted fraudsters to public burning or live burial.

Paragraph 5. Modern engineering has done little to replace manual harvesting. Iran currently dominates global trade, supplying over eighty-five percent of world saffron from its dry northeastern provinces. Saffron's distinct sensory character comes from three main phytochemicals: crocin lends its golden-yellow colour, picrocrocin generates its bitter undertone, and safranal produces its hay-like fragrance.

Paragraph 6. Looking ahead, climate scientists warn that erratic rainfall patterns and severe unseasonal frosts increasingly threaten traditional corm planting schedules in primary growing regions. Protecting this ancient spice will require balancing centuries-old manual skills with careful agricultural adaptation to shifting weather patterns.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...through the manual division and replanting of underground corms..."
Đoạn 2: Hoa nở lúc bình minh và nhanh chóng héo tàn (wilting rapidly) khi nắng lên.

q5.text: Cultivated saffron crocuses can survive without human help if planted in sunny fields.

steps: Đoạn 1: Cây vô sinh không tự tạo hạt hay sống ngoài tự nhiên được, sự sống còn phụ thuộc hoàn toàn vào người trồng.

q6.text: In classical Rome, saffron was scattered inside arenas to hide unpleasant odours.

steps: Đoạn 3: "...scattered across stone arenas to disguise the smell of gladiatorial contests..."

q7.text: The Safranschau tribunal in Nuremberg tested incoming spice batches chemically.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...empowered to seize and chemically test every batch entering city gates..."

q8.text: Safranal is extracted separately from saffron to manufacture commercial perfumes today.

steps: Đoạn 5: Chỉ giới thiệu safranal là chất tạo hương trong nghệ tây, không nói có tách riêng để làm nước hoa thương mại ngày nay hay không.

q9.text: Why must saffron pickers finish their work before sunrise?
options: A. Wild birds eat the red stigmas once daylight arrives
B. Rising heat and sunlight quickly damage the flower's essential oils
C. Mechanical harvesters only operate safely during dark hours
D. Fresh blossoms stay completely closed until midday

steps: Đoạn 2: Nhiệt độ tăng và ánh nắng trực tiếp phá hủy các hợp chất bay hơi và làm giảm chất lượng tinh dầu.

q10.text: Why did medieval merchants soak saffron threads in honey or oil?
options: A. To preserve their bright golden colour during sea voyages
B. To make cheap marigold petals taste pleasantly bitter
C. To artificially raise the weight of their shipments
D. To help threads pass Nuremberg's chemical inspections

steps: Đoạn 4: "...soaked batches in honey or oil to artificially boost shipment weight..."

options: A. Competition from newly invented artificial spices
